title: A Letter to God
summary: Lencho, an industrious farmer whose house stands alone on the crest of a low hill, watches his field of ripe corn dotted with bean flowers and prays for a timely shower. His joy turns to despair when a sudden hailstorm destroys the entire crop, and with no human help in sight he writes a letter to God asking for a hundred pesos to sow his field again. The postmaster, a fat amiable fellow, laughs at the address at first but is so moved by the writer's faith that he gathers seventy pesos, contributes part of his own salary and signs the envelope 'God'. Lencho is not surprised at receiving money, only angry that thirty pesos are missing; he writes a second letter demanding the rest but insisting that it must not travel through the mail, for he is certain the post office employees are a bunch of crooks.

Values of hope, generosity and never shaking another's faith

sections.heading: About the Author
sections.para: Gregorio Lopez y Fuentes (1897-1966) was one of the foremost novelists and short story writers of Mexico. Born in Veracruz, he grew up close to the land and wrote with warmth about the peasants, farmers and simple village people of his country. He witnessed the Mexican Revolution and its aftermath, and this experience gave his writing both realism and deep sympathy for the poor. His most celebrated novel, 'El Indio', which presents the tragedy of the Indian people of Mexico, won the National Prize of Arts and Sciences in 1935. In 'A Letter to God' his style is plain and direct: the story moves quickly, humour and pathos sit side by side, and the reader judges the characters by what they do rather than by what they say.
points: The story 'A Letter to God' was written by Gregorio Lopez y Fuentes, a famous Mexican novelist and short story writer.
He wrote mainly about the struggles, poverty and simple faith of the peasants and farmers of rural Mexico.
His famous novel 'El Indio' won Mexico's National Prize of Arts and Sciences in 1935.
Having seen the Mexican Revolution and its effect on the countryside, he wrote with realism and sympathy for the poor.
His style is simple and direct, letting ordinary people reveal themselves through their actions.
In this story he blends humour with pathos to show how faith sustains a simple man in disaster.

A quality that arouses feelings of pity and sadness.
The currency of Mexico and other Latin American countries.

sections.examPointer: Author-based one markers and questions on the irony of the ending are common; remember the setting is rural Mexico and the money is counted in pesos.

sections.heading: Lencho's World: The House on the Hill
sections.para: Lencho was a hardworking farmer who lived on the crest of a low hill with his wife and children. His was the only house in the entire valley, a solitary home standing amid fields that stretched far below it. From the house one could see the river and the field of ripe corn dotted with bean flowers, and Lencho knew his land and its needs intimately. That year the crop promised a rich harvest; all the earth needed was a timely shower. Because the family lived alone, far from neighbours, their hopes and fears rested on the sky above them. This setting matters greatly: the isolation of the house explains why, when disaster struck, Lencho turned not to any human being but straight to God, whose address he wrote on an envelope with perfect confidence.
points: Lencho's house stood on the crest of a low hill, and it was the only house in the entire valley.
Below the hill lay the river and the field of ripe corn dotted with bean flowers, promising a good harvest.
Lencho is described as 'an ox of a man', working like an animal in the fields, sowing and tending his crop.
The family lived in isolation, so they depended on the sky and on their own labour for survival.
Lencho's world was small and simple: wife, children, corn, beans and the mercy of the weather.
The solitary setting prepares us for the most unusual act of the story, a letter addressed simply to God.

keyTerms.meaning: The top of a hill, where Lencho's house stood.
Low land between hills; Lencho's house was the only one in the entire valley.
Matured maize crop ready for harvest, dotted with bean flowers.
Alone, without company; Lencho's family lived in solitude.
A metaphor for a man who works as hard and patiently as an ox.

sections.trick: One house, one hill, one hope: crest of a low hill, only house in the valley, only hope in God.
sections.examPointer: One markers often ask about the location of Lencho's house and the crop he grew; quote 'the field of ripe corn dotted with bean flowers' for accuracy.

sections.heading: The Rain of Joy and the Hailstorm of Ruin
sections.para: Throughout the morning Lencho studied the north-east sky and saw huge mountains of clouds gathering, so he told his wife they would really get some water now. When the first drops fell, the whole family rejoiced: the boys ran out to bathe in the rain, and Lencho counted the drops as new coins, the big ones as ten-cent pieces and the little ones as fives. But suddenly a strong wind began to blow and large hailstones came down along with the rain. They truly resembled new silver coins, they fell for a full hour, and the field turned white as if it had been covered with salt. The corn was destroyed, the bean flowers were gone and the leaves of the trees were stripped bare. Lencho said sorrowfully that even a plague of locusts would have left more than the hail had left.
points: Lencho looked at the north-east, saw huge mountains of clouds and exclaimed, 'Now we're really going to get some water, woman.'
The falling raindrops were compared to new coins: the big drops as ten-cent pieces and the little ones as fives.
The boys ran out into the rain to bathe while the woman stood preparing dinner, watching happily.
Suddenly a strong wind blew and huge hailstones fell along with the rain for a full hour.
The hailstones truly resembled new silver coins, and the field lay white as if covered with salt.
The entire crop of corn and beans was destroyed, and even the trees were left without leaves.
Lencho remarked that a plague of locusts would have left more than the hailstorm had left.

keyTerms.meaning: A heavy fall of rain that Lencho's crop needed badly.
A storm in which pellets of frozen rain fall and destroy standing crops.
Pellets of frozen rain, here compared to new silver coins.
Insects that fly in swarms and destroy crops.
A comparison using 'as' or 'like', as in raindrops like new coins.

sections.trick: COINS turn COLD: raindrops as copper coins, hailstones as silver coins, and one hour of hail turns the field to salt.
sections.examPointer: Extract-based questions usually come from the coin simile and the hailstorm paragraph; learn the exact images of ten-cent pieces, fives and new silver coins.

sections.heading: The Letter to God and the Postmaster's Reply
sections.para: With the crop gone, the family faced hunger, and Lencho's single hope was the help of God, who he firmly believed sees everything, even what is deep in one's conscience. He wrote a letter asking for a hundred pesos, enough to sow the field again and to live until the new crop came, and marked the envelope 'To God'. At the post office the postman laughed heartily and carried the letter to the postmaster, a fat, amiable fellow who too broke out laughing; but he soon turned serious and said he wished he had the faith of the man who wrote it. Not wanting Lencho's faith to be shaken, he collected seventy pesos, gave part of his own salary, persuaded employees and friends to contribute for an act of charity, signed the envelope 'God' and had the money delivered.
points: After the hailstorm Lencho's soul was filled with sadness, and his only hope was the help of God.
He wrote that if God did not help, his family would go hungry that year, and asked for a hundred pesos to sow the field again.
He was confident that God sees everything, even what is in one's conscience, and could not deny him what he asked.
The postman picked up the letter, laughed heartily at the address and showed it to the postmaster.
The postmaster laughed at first, then turned serious and resolved to answer the letter to keep the writer's faith alive.
He gave part of his own salary, collected money from employees and friends, and managed only seventy pesos.
He placed the money in an envelope addressed to Lencho and signed it with the single word 'God'.

keyTerms.meaning: The inner awareness of right and wrong; God, Lencho believes, sees every conscience.
Communication by letters; the postmaster jokes about starting up a correspondence with God.
Help given to the needy without expecting anything in return.
Friendly and good-natured, the postmaster's nature.
To decide firmly; the postmaster resolved to reply to the letter.

sections.trick: Two letters, one faith: letter one asks for 100, the gift is 70 signed 'God', letter two demands 30 and blames the helpers.
sections.examPointer: Remember the exact figures asked, sent and suspected (100, 70, 30) and the postmaster's wish to have such faith; these are constant MCQ and extract sources.

sections.heading: Character Sketch of Lencho
sections.para: Lencho deserves to be remembered as an 'ox of a man', simple, honest and tremendously hardworking. His whole life revolved around his field, and when the hail destroyed everything his sorrow was the sorrow of a worker whose labour has been wiped out overnight. His most striking quality is his faith: he writes to God as confidently as a child writes to a parent, asks for exact help and never doubts that the answer will come by post. Yet his faith is naive; he cannot imagine that people, not God, have sent the money. When he finds only seventy pesos, his trust in God remains untouched while his suspicion falls on the post office employees, whom he calls a bunch of crooks. Lencho is therefore at once noble in his faith and blind in his ingratitude, and that mixture makes him unforgettable.
points: Hardworking: he worked like an ox in his fields, ploughing, sowing and protecting his crop.
Faithful: he believed that God sees everything and would certainly answer his letter with help.
Simple and innocent: he never wondered how a letter could reach God without an address, or where the money came from.
Responsible: his first worry was his family, for whom he asked money to resow the field and survive till the harvest.
Ungrateful and suspicious: he accused the very people who helped him, calling them a bunch of crooks.
Confident to the point of arrogance: he instructed God to send the rest of the money by other means.
His faith stays firm throughout; only his faith in human beings collapses, which is the story's sharpest irony.

keyTerms.meaning: Hardworking and diligent, like Lencho in his field.
Innocent and unsophisticated, unable to see how things really work.
Lack of thankfulness; Lencho's fault towards his helpers.
Hopefulness about the future; his plan to sow again shows it.
A gang of thieves; Lencho's unfair label for the post office employees.

sections.trick: Lencho = OX + OWL: an ox in the field but an owl-blind judge of people, faithful to God and faithless to men.
sections.examPointer: Character sketches of Lencho are favourite 5 markers; support every quality with one incident, especially the two letters and the count of seventy pesos.

sections.heading: Character Sketch of the Postmaster
sections.para: The postmaster is the quiet hero of the story, a man whose humour turns into kindness. At first he is amused, for a letter addressed simply to God makes a fat, amiable man laugh heartily. But the depth of the farmer's faith touches him, and he decides to reply so that the writer's faith in God is not shaken. He cannot raise a hundred pesos, yet he quietly gives part of his own salary, gathers contributions from employees and friends, and sends seventy pesos signed with the single word 'God'. He seeks no credit, expects no thanks and receives only insult when Lencho accuses the post office of theft. Through him the story teaches that goodness often works anonymously, and that the noblest charity is the kind that protects another person's hope.
points: Amiable and jocular: a fat, friendly man who laughs heartily at the strange letter addressed to God.
Sensitive: he turns serious on reading the letter and wishes he had the writer's faith.
Compassionate: he resolves to send money so that Lencho's faith in God is not shaken.
Generous: he gives part of his own salary and appeals to employees and friends for an act of charity.
Honest in intention: he could collect only seventy pesos but sends all he can, signing it 'God'.
Selfless: he expects no thanks, tells Lencho nothing and bears the insult of the second letter silently.
He represents ordinary human beings through whom God's kindness reaches the poor.

keyTerms.meaning: The ability to feel another person's suffering, shown by the postmaster.
Willingness to give freely of one's money and effort.
Thinking of others before oneself, without seeking praise.
The belief the postmaster tries to protect when he answers the letter.
Kindly goodwill towards others, the spirit of his gift.

sections.trick: The postmaster PLAYS and then PAYS: he laughs first, then lends part of his salary to keep a stranger's faith alive.
sections.examPointer: Questions such as 'How did the postmaster keep Lencho's faith alive?' are asked for 2 to 5 marks; always mention seventy pesos and the single signature 'God'.

sections.heading: Themes and Message
sections.para: The central theme of the story is faith: the pure, unquestioning faith of a simple farmer in a God who answers letters. Closely linked is the theme of human kindness, shown by the postmaster and his colleagues, who become the hands through which God seems to act. The story is also a study in irony, for the very office that helps Lencho is accused by him of theft, and the man whose faith is praised shows deep suspicion of his fellow human beings. There is a further theme of the helplessness of the farmer, whose survival depends on weather he cannot control. The message is clear: never let anyone's faith be shaken, respond to another's need with quiet generosity, and remember that hope and charity together can rebuild what disaster destroys.
points: Faith in God: the story celebrates the deep, childlike faith of a poor farmer who believes God will answer by post.
Human kindness: the postmaster proves that God often works through compassionate human beings.
Irony and humour: the man helped by the post office calls its employees crooks, which is the central irony.
The contrast between spiritual faith and worldly suspicion brings out the innocence of simple village people.
The helplessness of farmers is highlighted, as their entire life depends on the mercy of the weather.
The message: never shake anyone's faith, because faith gives hope and strength to face disaster.

keyTerms.meaning: A feeling of doubting someone; Lencho's baseless doubt about his helpers.
Sympathy for the suffering of others, shown by the post office staff.
The confident expectation of good, which keeps Lencho planning a new sowing.
Simple purity of mind, free from cunning or worldly wisdom.
The unexpected contrast between the kindness of the staff and the insult they receive.

sections.trick: FAITH up, HAIL down, POSTMASTER kind, LENCHO blind: faith rises, the crop falls, kindness acts and innocence misjudges.
sections.examPointer: Questions such as 'What is the message of the story?' or 'Bring out the irony' are asked as 2 to 3 markers; quote the 'bunch of crooks' line for effect.

sections.heading: Important Incidents in Sequence
sections.para: Learning the story as a chain of incidents makes every extract question easy. Lencho watches the clouds from his hilltop and greets the first rain with joy, counting drops like coins. One hour of hail reduces the promised harvest to a white, salted field, and the family's talk of hunger drives him to write his first letter of one hundred pesos. The letter reaches the post office, where laughter gives way to a serious plan; seventy pesos travel back in an envelope signed 'God'. The count, the anger and the accusation follow at once, and the second letter asks for the missing thirty pesos while refusing the mail as a means. Each incident supplies one quotation, one emotion and one possible question, so memorising the chain covers the whole chapter efficiently.
points: Incident one: Lencho, an ox of a man, looks at the north-east clouds and predicts rain for his ripe corn.
Incident two: the joyful rain and the coin simile, with the boys bathing and the woman calling the drops new coins.
Incident three: the hour-long hailstorm that leaves the field white as salt and destroys the entire crop.
Incident four: the writing and posting of the first letter asking God for a hundred pesos.
Incident five: the post office scene of laughter, the postmaster's serious resolve and the collection of seventy pesos.
Incident six: Lencho counts the money, grows angry, and writes the second letter calling the employees a bunch of crooks.

keyTerms.meaning: The order of events in a story, from rain to ruin to reply to rage.
The paper cover carrying the money, signed 'God' by the postmaster.
A short passage from the text set as a question in the board paper.
The point of highest tension, here Lencho's anger at the incomplete sum.

sections.trick: R-H-L-G-A: Rain, Hail, Letter, Gift, Accusation; five beats cover the whole story.
sections.examPointer: Chronology-based MCQs ask what happened first or last; keep the order rain, hail, letter one, seventy pesos, letter two firmly in mind.

sections.heading: Value Points and Vocabulary
sections.para: The chapter rewards students who carry its values and its vocabulary together. On the value side, remember that true faith is total, that hope keeps a ruined family alive, and that the best charity is quiet, prompt and without expectation of reward. On the language side, master the word meanings that examiners pick for one markers: crest, downpour, hailstone, locusts, conscience, resolved, amiable and the expression 'a bunch of crooks'. Practise using phrases like 'an ox of a man' and 'the favour of God' inside your answers, because precise quotation from the text is always rewarded in board evaluation. A single answer that combines one incident, one value and one exact phrase will score higher than a page of vague writing.
points: True faith is total: Lencho never doubts God, only the human post office, and this keeps him hopeful.
Helping hands: the postmaster proves that goodness often travels unseen, like a letter signed 'God'.
Value of hope: after total loss, hope alone keeps the family alive and planning the next sowing.
Vocabulary: crest (top of a hill), downpour (heavy rain), hailstone (pellet of frozen rain), locusts (crop-destroying insects).
Vocabulary: pesos (Latin American money), ox of a man (very hardworking man), amiable (friendly).
Vocabulary: conscience (inner sense of right and wrong), resolved (decided firmly), a bunch of crooks (a gang of thieves).

keyTerms.meaning: Thankfulness, the value Lencho fails to show.
The strength to start again, seen in Lencho's plan to resow.
Respect for hard work, reflected in the image of Lencho the ox of a man.
Selfless concern for others, the postmaster's defining virtue.

sections.trick: Value triple for any answer: Faith, Hope, Charity; vocabulary pair: crest of a hill, bunch of crooks.
sections.examPointer: Value-based questions of 3 to 4 marks ask what the story teaches about faith or kindness; answer with the postmaster's example and Lencho's hope of resowing.

boardQuestions.question: What did Lencho write in his first letter to God?
boardQuestions.answer: In his first letter Lencho told God that if He did not help him, his family and he would go hungry that year. He requested a hundred pesos, which he needed to sow his field again after the hailstorm and to live until the new crop came, because the hail had left nothing behind.

boardQuestions.question: Why did Lencho compare the raindrops to new coins? What happened immediately after this happy moment?
boardQuestions.answer: Lencho compared the raindrops to new coins because rain at that moment meant money: a timely downpour would ripen his corn and beans and become a rich harvest, which is the farmer's cash. To him the big drops were ten-cent pieces and the little ones were fives, so even the smallest shower looked like wealth falling from the sky. Immediately after this happy moment, a strong wind began to blow and huge hailstones fell along with the rain for a whole hour, covering the field as if with salt and destroying the entire crop of corn and beans, leaving the family staring at hunger.

boardQuestions.question: How did the post office employees react to Lencho's letter, and why did the postmaster decide to answer it?
boardQuestions.answer: The postman first picked up the letter and laughed heartily at an envelope addressed simply to God, and the postmaster too broke out laughing when he saw it. However, the postmaster quickly turned serious; tapping the letter on his desk, he said that he wished he had the faith of the man who wrote it. He then resolved to answer the letter, though not in his own name, because he did not want to shake the writer's faith in God. For this act of charity he gave part of his own salary, collected contributions from his employees and friends, and sent all he could gather, seventy pesos, signed 'God'.

boardQuestions.question: Draw a character sketch of Lencho in the light of the story 'A Letter to God'.
boardQuestions.answer: Lencho is presented as an 'ox of a man', a poor but industrious farmer who works like an animal in his fields and knows that his survival depends on his labour and the mercy of the sky. He is optimistic by nature: when clouds gather in the north-east he happily predicts rain, and he counts the first drops like new coins, dreaming of the harvest they promise. Disaster, however, tests him. After the hour-long hailstorm destroys everything, his soul fills with sadness, yet he does not collapse; instead his deep, childlike faith rises, and he writes a letter to God with the confidence of a son writing to a father, certain that God sees everything, even what lies in one's conscience. His faith is total but naive, for he never wonders how a letter can reach God without an address, or how money can come down from heaven by post. When seventy pesos arrive, he is not surprised, because his confidence in God never wavers; instead he becomes angry at the missing thirty and accuses the post office employees of being a bunch of crooks. Here lies his tragic flaw: his faith in God is blind, but his faith in humanity is absent, and he repays secret charity with insult. Lencho thus remains a memorable mixture of hard work, hope, innocence and ingratitude, a simple man whose noble faith and unjust suspicion together create the story's unforgettable irony.

boardQuestions.question: Give a character sketch of the postmaster in 'A Letter to God'.
boardQuestions.answer: The postmaster of the small village post office is a fat, amiable fellow, cheerful by nature, who first appears laughing heartily at the absurd letter addressed to God. That laughter, however, is only the surface of his character. When he reads the letter properly, the depth of the farmer's faith moves him, and he says that he wishes he had such faith himself. From amusement he passes to action: he decides to reply so that the writer's faith in God may not be shaken, and this decision reveals his compassion and respect for another person's belief. He cannot gather the full hundred pesos, but he gives part of his own salary and persuades his employees and friends to contribute for an act of charity, finally sending seventy pesos in an envelope signed with the single word 'God'. He does all this anonymously, seeking neither credit nor thanks, and he receives in return the bitter accusation that his staff are a bunch of crooks; yet the story tells of no complaint from him. The postmaster therefore stands for quiet, practical goodness: he cannot perform miracles, but he becomes the miracle for a stranger. His character teaches that kindness does not need applause, that faith in humanity can protect faith in God, and that a little generosity, given without show, can keep hope alive in a ruined household.

boardQuestions.question: Justify the title 'A Letter to God'. What does the story suggest about faith and charity?
boardQuestions.answer: The title 'A Letter to God' is fully justified because the entire story revolves around two letters written by Lencho and posted to no earthly address but to God himself. The first letter is born of absolute faith: a farmer ruined by hail believes that God, who sees everything including the conscience, will surely read his request and send a hundred pesos by post. The letter becomes a test of that faith, and the answer comes, not from heaven, but from the postmaster, who raises seventy pesos and signs it 'God'. The second letter completes the irony: the same faith that asked for a hundred now demands the missing thirty, while refusing to let them travel through a post office full of 'crooks'. Through this simple exchange the story suggests that faith gives the poor the strength to face disaster, and that God often answers letters through kind human beings; the postmaster becomes God's unseen hand. It also warns that charity must be patient with ingratitude, for the giver receives insult while the receiver stays innocent. Thus the title is apt: one letter creates the miracle of kindness, and a second letter exposes the blindness of simple faith, making 'A Letter to God' a perfect name for a story about prayer, charity and irony.

boardQuestions.question: Read the extract and answer the questions: With a strong wind beginning to blow, huge hailstones began to fall along with the rain. The hail did not stop for a full hour, and the field was covered as if with salt. The corn was totally destroyed; the flowers were gone from the plants. Lencho's soul was filled with sadness. (a) What images does the writer use to describe the hail? (b) What was the immediate effect of the hailstorm on the family? (c) What single hope remained in the hearts of the family?
boardQuestions.answer: 1) (a) The writer uses the simile of salt: the field lay white 'as if it had been covered with salt'; earlier the falling hailstones are compared to new silver coins thrown from the sky. 2) The images of whiteness and silver show both the beauty and the terror of the hail, which looks precious while it destroys everything. 3) (b) The immediate effect was total ruin: the crop of ripe corn was completely destroyed, the bean flowers were gone and the trees stood stripped of leaves, so the family faced the prospect of hunger for the whole year. 4) Lencho's sorrow is personal and bitter; he says even a plague of locusts would have left more than the hail left. 5) (c) The single hope remaining in the hearts of all who lived in that solitary house was the help of God, in whom Lencho had complete and unquestioning faith, and this hope leads directly to the writing of the letter that gives the story its title.

boardQuestions.question: 'Faith in God and kindness among human beings are the two pillars of the story A Letter to God.' Discuss with examples. What values should we learn from it?
boardQuestions.answer: The story rests on two pillars that support each other. The first is faith: Lencho, ruined by the hailstorm, does not lose heart but writes to God with the calm certainty of a son, believing that God sees everything and will send a hundred pesos. This faith is pure but naive, and it survives even the shock of receiving only seventy pesos. The second pillar is human kindness: the postmaster, moved by the farmer's letter, gives part of his salary and collects seventy pesos from willing colleagues, signing the envelope 'God' so that the stranger's faith is not shaken. He asks for nothing, and the thanks he gets is the insult of 'a bunch of crooks', yet his charity stands as the real miracle of the story. The values we should learn are: never mock or shake another person's faith, help the needy quietly and promptly, accept gratitude or insult with equal patience, and preserve hope in the worst disaster, because faith and kindness together can rebuild what misfortune destroys.
